imageCaption: Aaliyah stands in Mrs. Chen's bodega, surrounded by forty-two bundles of flowers that shouldn't exist, comparing her hand-drawn map of fourteen addresses to Mrs. Chen's delivery checklist. Outside the window, the neighborhood is walking in slow deliberate arcs, carrying flowers like pilgrims.
text:
The bodega was impossible again.

This time, the impossibility wasn't flowers. The flowers had already happened—they'd done their job, anchored the first table, proved that glitches responded to emotional completion. Now they were gone, delivered, placed in strategic positions across the neighborhood like time-stabilization devices made of petals and stems.

The new impossibility was the order forms.

"This isn't real," Aaliyah said. She was standing in front of Mrs. Chen's counter, holding a sheaf of papers that shouldn't exist. "These are delivery orders. For sancocho. For tomorrow. From addresses that weren't on the original list."

Mrs. Chen was behind the register with the expression of someone who'd run a bodega for thirty years and had learned to accept that some days the universe reorganized itself. She didn't look surprised so much as vindicated.

"They came in starting at four PM," she said. "People texting, calling, one gentleman came in person to ask if you were going to feed more than one block. Apparently word travels faster than time in this neighborhood." She gestured at the papers. "Twenty-three new addresses. All requesting sancocho. All asking if flowers could be included."

Elijah appeared from behind a cereal display with the timing of someone who'd been conducting reconnaissance. "The flowers want to help," he announced. He was holding a piece of deli cheese shaped like Switzerland. "Sully told me. The flowers didn't stop stuttering because we put them down. They stopped stuttering because they were finally being useful. And now they want more people to know that."

"That's not how flowers work," Aaliyah said automatically.

"That's not how anything works," Elijah replied. "And yet."

He was right. Somehow, this was exactly how flowers worked now. This was exactly how the frequency worked now. One table, one glitch stabilized, one moment of beautiful completion—and suddenly the neighborhood understood what was being built. Suddenly there were twenty-three new addresses, each with their own specific gravity, all asking to be part of the second Sunday that hadn't even been scheduled yet.

Marco appeared in the bodega doorway like he'd been tracking the situation and had arrived at important conclusions. He was holding his phone with the intensity of someone documenting something that mattered.

"The internet is starting to glitch around this," he said without preamble. "People are posting about the bodega's flowers. About the brownstone gathering. The posts keep disappearing and reappearing. One person described it as 'the timeline trying to decide if this is real enough to keep.' Are you going to do this? Sancocho for twenty-three more addresses?"

"I don't know," Aaliyah said. And she meant it. The truth was complicated. One table had nearly killed her with anxiety. One table had triggered a glitch so intense that she'd spent the entire gathering convinced the timeline was going to unravel. And one table had worked. The frequency had held. The neighborhood had arrived.

But twenty-three tables was a different category of impossible.

Luisana appeared, carrying coffee in a paper cup that might have been from this bodega or from yesterday or from some timeline-splinter where she'd been planning this exact expansion three days ago. Her journal was tucked under her arm.

"Show me the list," she said.

Aaliyah handed over the papers. Luisana studied them with the focus of someone reading a document that meant something. She made notes in her journal—not casual notes, but the kind of notes that were building toward something. After a long moment, she looked up.

"These addresses," she said. "They're not random. Look at the clusters. They form a pattern."

Aaliyah took the list back. Luisana was right. The addresses weren't scattered across the neighborhood. They were clustered in specific directions, specific blocks, creating a route that looked like—

"Like the route to somewhere," Aaliyah said slowly. She pulled out her hand-drawn map. The original fourteen addresses were clustered on the south side of the neighborhood. The new twenty-three were moving north, northeast, in slow deliberate arcs that looked less like random requests and more like the timeline marking a path.

"Where are they pointing?" Marco asked.

Aaliyah traced the line with her finger. If she extended the pattern, if she followed the arc that the neighborhood was unconsciously creating through their requests, it would point toward—

"Riverside Park," she said. "They're pointing toward Riverside Park."

"Why would the timeline want you in Riverside Park?" Elijah asked. He'd abandoned his Switzerland cheese and was now studying the map with the intensity of someone who understood that questions that sounded childish often contained profound answers.

"Because," Luisana said carefully, "that's where we haven't been yet. That's where the pattern becomes clear."

Anthony appeared in the bodega entrance with the timing of people showing up when their family was actively trying to solve a problem. He had his phone in his hand and the expression of someone who'd been noticing something.

"Hey," he said. "The license plate collection. I need to show you something."

He pulled out the small roll-up pegboard he carried everywhere. The collection had grown since they'd arrived in New York—there were plates from Argentina, from Iceland, from Tokyo, from every place they'd accidentally stabilized a glitch. The plates were organized in the order of their travels, a geographical map of chaos slowly becoming purpose.

But one plate was glowing.

Not metaphorically. There was an actual luminescence coming from the pegboard, centered on a single spot. Anthony tilted it and the glow shifted, revealing something underneath the New York license plate—something that looked like a shadow of a different plate, a different location, flickering between visibility and absence.

"This started happening about an hour ago," Anthony said. "Right after the flower delivery. I thought I was imagining it at first, but it's getting clearer. It's like the collection is showing me something the timeline wants me to see."

"What's the next location?" Aaliyah asked. Her voice was very steady. She was training herself to ask the important questions without falling apart while asking them.

Anthony studied the glowing plate. "Can't quite see it yet," he said. "But it's definitely pointing north. Definitely pointing toward—"

"Riverside Park," Elijah finished. He said it like a prophecy. Like the universe had told him what was coming and he was just confirming what he already knew.

The bodega seemed to hold its breath. Mrs. Chen was watching from behind her counter. Marco was documenting. Luisana was writing. Anthony was studying his impossible license plate. Sully—who had appeared from somewhere, as Sully did—was sitting at attention, clearly aware that something was becoming visible.

"We can't feed this many people," Aaliyah said. It was a fact, not an argument. "We don't have the infrastructure. We don't have—"

"We have neighbors," Luisana said quietly. "We have a bodega owner who makes flowers appear. We have a community that's already learning the frequency. And we have a timeline that's pointing us somewhere specific." She paused. "You've mapped the pattern. You understand what's being asked. The question isn't whether you can do this. The question is whether you trust that the neighborhood is as ready as you are."

Aaliyah looked at the faces around her. Mrs. Chen, who'd somehow manifested flowers. Marco, who documented chaos like it was the most beautiful language. Elijah, who always seemed to be standing exactly where the truth was about to appear. Anthony, holding his collection of plates like it was a map to somewhere that mattered. Luisana, writing the story of what her family had accidentally begun.

And Sully, sitting perfectly still, already pointing toward whatever came next.

"Okay," Aaliyah said. It was very quiet. It was very certain. "Okay. We go to Riverside Park. We feed whoever asks. And we figure out what the timeline is trying to show us."

"That's my girl," Anthony said.

Outside, the August evening was settling in. The neighborhood was walking in slow deliberate arcs, carrying flowers like pilgrims. And somewhere in the distance, Riverside Park was waiting to become whatever it was supposed to be when a family and a neighborhood together decided to make it beautiful.
